# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Critical Read: Two-Year Follow-up of Varden and Halden

**Bottom line:** This is the strongest document of the five, and it settles the main open questions from the previous four. The arithmetic checks out, the comparisons are mostly like for like, and the claims are generally well calibrated. Four things need qualifying:
- The summary compares two different hours measures, which makes the decline look larger than it was.
- Two control offices cut their own meetings during the follow-up, which shrinks the measured treatment effect.
- The registered mediation test reuses the offices that generated the hypothesis, so "confirms" is too strong.
- Whether meeting time counts in the hours denominator affects how the mediation result should be read.

## What checks out

- **Per-hour figures:**
  - Timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8%.
  - System logs: 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5%.
- **Confidence intervals:** they are symmetric on the log scale. The per-hour interval matches the per-FTE interval divided by the hours ratio (0.920 / 0.89 = +3.4%, 1.012 / 0.89 = +13.7%).
- **Meetings:** treated offices fell by 3.5 hours and control offices by 0.2, a difference of 3.3 hours. This matches the nine-month figure, and the new baseline data answer my earlier concern that meeting time had no baseline.
- **Mediation shares:** 47% + 18% + 35% = 100%.
- **Counter staffing estimate:** restoring staffed hours after a 17% cut in actual hours, with a 6.7% per-hour gain, requires 1 / (0.83 × 1.067) ≈ 1.13, about +13% staff. That is consistent with the 12% quoted. A 9% rise in cost per contact implies labour is roughly three-quarters of costs, which is plausible but not stated.
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866 (−13.4%), and 96.8 / 0.866 = +11.8%.

## Strengths

- **Standards met:** randomised comparison, record-based output, a stricter hours measure and two-year follow-up. These are the standards Varga and Holm called for.
- **Mediation registered in advance:** the analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were known, with the mediators and the outcome specified.
- **Unrecorded work:** the system-log measure addresses it directly. It shows slightly more work than timesheets, which is the expected direction.
- **Measure comparisons:** the body text correctly identifies 12.5% → 9.8% as the like-for-like comparison.
- **Counter arm:** its ending is reported transparently, with waits compared against control rather than before and after, fixing a weakness of the nine-month report.
- **Halden continuers:** they are described honestly as "survivors twice over".
- **Meeting audit:** the unplanned observation is reported cautiously, and the authors say plainly that the trial cannot separate reorganisation from the hours cut.
- **Meta-analysis check:** the four long-follow-up studies in the meta-analysis turn out to be uncontrolled and based on scheduled hours. This confirms the concern raised in my previous review.

## Problems

**1. The summary overstates the decline.**
The summary sets 12.5% (timesheets, nine months) against 8.5% (logs, 24 months), which suggests a drop of about a third. On the same measure, the drop is 12.5% → 9.8%, about a fifth. There is no log-based figure at nine months to compare. And if logs were available for the baseline (needed for a log-based difference-in-differences), a nine-month log estimate should have been possible too. The summary should lead with the like-for-like comparison.

**2. Control-office meeting cuts shrink the measured effect.**
- **What happened:** two of the seven control offices cut meetings in month 15 and gained 4.1% per hour.
- **Effect on the control average:** if offices are of similar size, that raises the control group's average by about 1.2% (2/7 × 4.1%).
- **Effect on the estimate:** that alone could account for roughly 1 of the 2.7 points of apparent decline.

So part of the "fading" may be the control group improving, not the treated offices falling back. The authors present this observation only as evidence that reorganisation without an hours cut might work. They don't note that it also contaminates the trial comparison.

**3. The decline itself is uncertain.**
The nine-month and 24-month intervals overlap almost entirely (+6.9 to +18.4 and +4.6 to +15.2). No test of the change is reported. "Declined by about a quarter" describes the point estimates. The data are also consistent with little or no decline. What the data do rule out is a decline to zero.

**4. The mediation test is less of a confirmation than the summary says.**
- **Same offices:** the registered test uses the same seven treated offices whose month-six pattern prompted the hypothesis. It is new data over time, not new offices, so this is not independent replication.
- **Sample size:** "a larger sample of office-months" adds observations but not independent units. Treatment was assigned to 14 offices, and an interval of 28–66% looks narrow for that. The paper should state how clustering was handled.
- **Confounding:** the authors acknowledge that unmeasured confounding between the mediators and the outcome is possible. Managers who cut meetings may differ in other ways that also raise output.

"Supports" would be accurate. "Confirms", as used in the summary, overstates it.

**5. Meeting time and the hours measure.**
- **Meetings counted in hours (timesheets):** removing meeting hours that produce no measured output raises output per hour by arithmetic alone. That is real, since low-value time was cut, but it is an accounting effect rather than a change in how people work.
- **Meetings excluded from hours (case-system log time):** a meetings effect on output per log hour would then have to work through other channels, such as fewer interruptions and longer focus blocks.

The paper uses log hours but doesn't say whether log time includes meetings. The answer changes what "meetings explain 47%" means.

**6. Smaller points**
- **Halden subset:** only 14 of 23 organisations responded, and nothing is reported about the 9 that didn't.
- **Reverters' output:** the three reverters had record-based output of 88–91. That is evidence about why organisations revert.
- **Marketing agency:** a discretionary-sector agency reverted over client deadlines. This supports coding by whether work depends on presence or deadlines rather than by sector.
- **Authorship:** Okafor, the Halden lead author, is a co-author. The findings don't favour Halden's original claims, so this doesn't look like a problem, but it is worth stating.
- **Cost per case:** output per FTE of −3.4% at full pay means cost per case rose by about 3.5%, plus any claimed overtime. Lower sick leave (−27%) and resignations (4.1% vs 7.9%) offset part of that, and the paper could put rough figures on both.
- **Appeal overturn rates:** these are still reported without confidence intervals.

## Assessment of the claims about earlier papers

- **Varga and Holm, "entirely an artifact":** fairly refuted. An 8.5% gain (3.4 to 13.8) under their own recommended standards is hard to dismiss. Their novelty concern was partly right: some fading is possible, though not to zero, and their prediction of a return to baseline at month ten is clearly wrong. Their rejection of the meetings hypothesis also looks wrong, subject to point 4.
- **Achterberg et al., "no sign of decay":** fairly refuted. Their long-follow-up subgroup consisted entirely of studies with the design features they themselves found to inflate effects.

## How the evidence stands after five documents

| Question | Best current answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, best evidence | About 8.5–10% at 24 months (randomised, records, log or timesheet hours). |
| Durability | Holds to 24 months. Possibly some decline from 12.5%, partly explained by control offices improving. Beyond 24 months is unknown. |
| Output per worker, discretionary | Slightly down (−3.4%, CI −8.0 to +1.2). The hours cut is mostly, not fully, offset. |
| Coverage-bound work | Not viable without about 12% more staff and about 9% higher cost per contact. The county ended the arm. |
| Mechanism | Meeting cuts are the largest measured pathway (about half), fatigue is smaller (about a fifth), and about a third is unexplained. |
| Can reorganisation alone deliver the gain? | Open. Weakly suggestive evidence from two control offices. Needs a trial arm that reorganises without cutting hours. |
| Wellbeing and retention | Sick leave about −27% and resignations roughly halved, sustained at 24 months. |
| Remaining gaps | Private-sector randomised trials, manufacturing and shift work, follow-up beyond 24 months, and a trial arm that reorganises without cutting hours. |

The most important design for the next trial is three arms: reduced hours, reorganisation (meeting audits and similar) at full hours, and control. That would show whether employers need the hours cut or only the clean-up it triggers.
